The Odyssey. An ancient Greek epic poem in dactylic hexameter, traditionally attributed to Homer, and a companion work to the Iliad. Spanning twenty-four books and roughly twelve thousand lines, the epic chronicles the ten-year nostos, or homecoming, of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, as he struggles to return from Troy after its fall, encountering divine obstacles, monsters, and moral trials that test his wit and resolve. The poem is simultaneously a hero's journey of adventure and suffering, a domestic tragedy exploring loyalty and fidelity, and a meditation on mortality and the price of fame, establishing the archetype of the quest narrative that has endured through all Western literature.

The epic begins in medias res with Odysseus trapped on the island of Ogygia as the captive and desired immortal husband of the nymph Calypso, who refuses to release him. While Odysseus is away, his wife Penelope is besieged by suitors in Ithaca, whom she holds at bay by claiming she will marry one after completing a funeral shroud for Odysseus's father Laertes, which she secretly unravels each night. The poem intercuts between Odysseus's journey and his son Telemachus's coming-of-age quest to find news of his father and assert his own manhood.

Odysseus blinds the Cyclops Polyphemus to escape his cave, but in doing so incurs the wrath of Poseidon, Polyphemus's father, who pursues Odysseus for the remainder of his journey. He encounters the lotus-eaters, whose narcotic flowers cause his men to forget home. He encounters the witch Circe, who transforms his men into swine, and the Sirens, whose deadly song he resists by having himself lashed to the mast. Odysseus navigates between the sea monsters Scylla and Charybdis, loses more men to a cannibalistic giant, and his crew's hunger leads them to slaughter Helios's sacred cattle, bringing divine punishment and death.

On Circe's advice, Odysseus journeys to the underworld, called the nekyia, to consult the blind prophet Tiresias, where he encounters the shades of his mother Anticleia and the spirit of Achilles. He is restored to his ship and finally reaches Ithaca, where he disguises himself as a beggar to scout the situation and reunite with his son. Odysseus reveals himself to Telemachus and uses an archery contest, stringing his great bow which only he can draw, to identify the suitors and slaughter them all. He reclaims his throne, re-establishes his marriage with Penelope, and restores order to Ithaca, earning a reprieve from his sufferings.

The Odyssey complements the Iliad by shifting from martial glory to domestic restoration and personal growth. While the Iliad celebrates the warrior's honor in death, the Odyssey celebrates survival, ingenuity, and the hero's return to family and civilization. The poem established the quest narrative as one of literature's enduring forms, the hero's journey through trials toward self-discovery and homecoming. It explores themes of loyalty, the costs of pride, and the human desire for recognition and legacy. The concept of nostos, the homecoming, became central to Greek identity, and the poem's portrayal of Odysseus as resourceful and clever, or metis, rather than merely strong elevated cunning as a form of heroism. It has been adapted, imitated, and reinterpreted countless times, from Dante to Joyce's Ulysses to modern film, proving its archetypal power.
